title: Function
source: Sample chapter written for testing. Replace it with your textbook (see README: Load your textbook).

pages.text: Introduction. A large program is easier to write, read and test when it is split into small named blocks of code. Such a block is called a subroutine. Subroutines are the basic building blocks of a program. In programming languages a subroutine is usually called a function. A function is a unit of code that does a particular job. Once written, a function can be used (called) many times from different parts of the program, so we do not need to repeat the same code. Advantages of functions: they reduce duplication of code, they make a large program easier to understand by breaking it into small parts, they make testing and correcting errors easier, and they allow code to be reused in other programs.

Function definition. A function definition gives the function a name, lists the inputs it needs, and contains the statements that do the work. Example in Python:

def rectangle_area(length, breadth):
    area = length * breadth
    return area

Here rectangle_area is the function name. length and breadth are parameters. The return statement sends the result back to the place where the function was called. Calling the function: print(rectangle_area(5, 3)) prints 15. The values 5 and 3 are arguments.

Parameters and arguments. Parameters are the variables written in the function definition. Arguments are the actual values passed to the function when it is called. In def add(a, b): a and b are parameters. In add(10, 20), 10 and 20 are arguments. Parameters may be written without a data type, and the language works out the type from the arguments, or with an explicit data type in some languages. Interface and implementation. An interface describes what a function or object does: its name, its inputs and the result it gives. An implementation is the actual code that carries out the work. A user only needs to know the interface to use a function; the implementation can be changed later without affecting the user. Example: a TV remote's buttons are the interface; the electronics inside are the implementation.

Pure and impure functions. A pure function always gives the same result for the same arguments, and it has no side effects: it does not change any variable or data outside itself. Example: def square(x): return x * x. square(4) is always 16. An impure function may give different results for the same arguments, or it changes something outside itself (a side effect), such as a global variable, a file, or printing to the screen. Example: import random; def roll(): return random.randint(1, 6) gives a different value each time. Another example:

count = 0
def increment():
    global count
    count = count + 1
    return count

increment() changes the global variable count, so it is impure. Pure functions are easier to test and to reason about.

questions.question: Small named blocks of code that are the building blocks of a program are called:
questions.explanation: Subroutines (functions) are the basic building blocks of a program.

questions.question: In add(10, 20), what are 10 and 20?
questions.explanation: Values passed at the time of the call are arguments.

questions.question: What is printed?
The buttons on a TV remote are an example of:
questions.explanation: The interface is what the user sees and uses.

questions.question: Why is a function that changes a global variable called impure?
questions.answer: Because it has a side effect: it changes data outside the function.
questions.explanation: Changing something outside the function is a side effect, so it is impure.

questions.question: Which function is pure?
questions.explanation: square always gives the same result for the same input and has no side effects.
